title: Level 4 (Expert) - C-19
notes:
West leads the ♠7 against 4♥. East wins the ♠A and returns the suit. South knows that his ♠K will be ruffed out, but he should play the ♠K anyway, in order to preserve a small spade as a possible squeeze threat against East.

West ruffs and returns the ♦K. South still has 2 losers (1 in spades and 1 in diamonds). If West has the sole defensive guard against the ♦10, South should be able to arrange a double squeeze. East will have to guard spades and West diamonds. If South times the play properly, neither defender will be able to guard dummy's clubs.

West should be allowed to win the diamond trick to rectify the count to 1 loser. West will continue diamonds, the ♦A winning. South now runs his trumps.

On the play of the last trump, West must pitch a club to keep his diamond guard. Dummy's ♦10 is discarded and East is squeezed. He must keep his last spade and, therefore, he also will have to part with a club. As both defenders have abandoned clubs, the suit will run.

The squeeze would have been equally effective if either defender held the sole defensive guard in clubs. In this case the squeeze would have been a simple squeeze, not a double squeeze.

In every double squeeze, each defender is responsible for guarding a suit of his own (East guards spades, West guards diamonds). Both defenders share the control of a third suit. There must be at least 1 winner in the shared suit at the time of the squeeze. Double squeezes mature with 1 loser. Several forms of double squeeze exist. The above position is one of the easiest forms to recognize and execute.
